To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) cognitive reappraisal reduces negative affect and improves memory for negative stimuli, whereas expressive suppression reduces negative affect but impairs explicit memory for negative stimuli; (b) successful encoding during cognitive reappraisal was associated with increased co-activation of left inferior frontal gyris, amygdala and hippocampus, and (c) the amygdala and left inferior frontal gyras were associated with successful encoding of negative pictures across all conditions.

1) Cognitive reappraisal, but not expressive suppression, was associated with enhanced memory for negative pictures, relative to passive viewing; 2) The neural mechanisms underlying successful memory encoding during cognitive reappraisal included greater co-activation between the left inferior frontal cortex, amygdala and hippocampus.
reappraising negative stimuli leads to a reduction in negative emotion and an enhancement of memory.
